summary: Learners aged 12–13 explain conduction, convection and radiation qualitatively using the particle model, organised under one rule: a temperature difference drives energy from hotter to cooler until the difference disappears (thermal equilibrium). The central move is making the learner state explicitly WHAT moves in each case — energy handed along particles that vibrate about fixed positions (conduction), the bulk fluid physically circulating (convection), and an infrared wave that needs no medium and can cross even a vacuum (radiation) — and tying the rate of transfer to the size of the temperature difference. Activities span an interactive particle sandbox, a sorting/assessment check, a reference triptych, a Socratic misconception dialogue, and a spatial loop view, each with a distinct purpose.
misconceptions: 'Cold flows / cold gets in' — treating cold as a substance that travels. Energy only ever moves from hotter to cooler; a cold object gains energy, it does not emit cold.
'Heat rises' — over-generalised. It is warmed FLUID (less dense air/water) that rises in convection; heat itself has no inherent upward direction, and conduction/radiation are not 'up'.
Confusing temperature with heat / thermal energy — temperature measures average particle kinetic energy; a large warm object can hold more thermal energy than a small hot one.
'Metal is colder than wood' — objects in the same room are at the same temperature; metal merely conducts energy away from the hand faster, so it FEELS colder.
'Convection is heat moving through the liquid/gas' — in convection the fluid itself physically circulates; the energy is carried by moving matter, not passed through stationary matter.
'Radiation means nuclear / is only from very hot or dangerous things' — all objects emit and absorb infrared radiation at all times; it needs no medium and is not inherently harmful.
'Wool / a blanket / a coat gives out heat or warms things up' — insulators slow energy transfer; they do not generate heat (a blanket round ice keeps it cold).
Believing the rate of transfer is constant — it depends on the temperature difference, so a hot object cools quickly at first and ever more slowly as it nears equilibrium.
Assuming metals are the only conductors / that 'good conductor' and 'gets hot easily' are the same — conduction is about how fast energy passes through, not how hot a thing gets.

activities.title: Particle-level heat sandbox: what is moving in each mechanism?
steps: In a conduction mode, heat one end of a bar of fixed, jiggling particles and watch vibration energy pass along to neighbours; toggle 'metal' to add free electrons that carry energy far faster and compare how quickly the far end of a metal vs wooden bar warms.

In a convection mode, heat the bottom of a beaker or room of free fluid particles; follow a dyed blob or arrows as warmed fluid expands (its particles move further apart), becomes less dense and rises, then cools at the top, becomes denser and sinks, tracing a visible loop — then state in words whether the fluid itself moves or the heat passes through still fluid.

In a radiation mode, emit infrared arrows from a hot object across a gap, then use a 'remove the air / vacuum' toggle (an idealised model) and check whether the target still warms; compare a matt-black vs shiny target (the same surface types compared on a Leslie cube, which is usually used to show emission) and see that the matt-black target absorbs infrared faster.
Move one shared 'temperature difference' slider across all three modes and describe how the transfer rate changes as the gap widens and as the two sides drift toward equilibrium.

Use a side 'feel' panel: when metal and wood are at the SAME temperature and both are cooler than the hand, the hand loses warmth faster to the metal — put into words how sensation, temperature and rate differ.
activities.insight: Each mechanism is a different way the hotter-to-cooler rule is carried out, distinguished by what actually moves: energy along stationary particles, the circulating bulk fluid, or an EM wave needing no medium; transfer rate grows with the temperature difference and falls toward equilibrium.

activities.title: Sort and challenge: which mechanism, and what moves?
steps: Drag everyday examples into conduction / convection / radiation: metal spoon in soup, Sun warming skin, hot-air balloon, radiator warming a room, sea breeze — and for each state what is moving.

Predict what a thermometer (or thermal strip) reads on a metal spoon and a wooden spoon that have sat in the same room long enough to reach room temperature, then measure to check: the readings should be approximately the same, within measurement error.
Answer: 'Food in a freezer gets colder — is cold going into the food, or is energy leaving the food?' and justify using the hotter-to-cooler rule.
Explain why the metal spoon feels colder than the wooden one even though the measurements show approximately equal temperatures (both cooler than your hand).
Complete: 'energy travels from ___ to ___ until the temperature difference is ___'.
Order a cooling drink's transfer rate from fast to slow as the temperature gap shrinks.
activities.insight: The mechanism distinctions and the hotter-to-cooler rule can be applied to novel everyday cases; approximately equal readings show both spoons are at about the same (room) temperature, and the common cold-flows / heat-rises / metal-is-colder errors can be caught and corrected.

activities.title: Reference triptych: three mechanisms on tap
steps: Open three labelled panels (conduction / convection / radiation) and tap a region in each to reveal 'what moves' and a real example.
Use a flap that contrasts shiny vs matt surfaces (as on a Leslie cube) for emitting and absorbing infrared.
Return to this glossary while working in the sandbox to check a term or example.
activities.insight: The vocabulary, canonical pictures and real examples for each mechanism can be recalled and used as a reference layer.

activities.title: Thermal-imaging engineer: predict and justify
steps: Respond to an in-role engineer who asks for predictions and reasons: 'Will the vacuum stop the heat? Why?', 'Why does the metal feel colder?', 'You said cold gets in — what is actually moving?'

Tackle the engineer's counterexample: on a hot day a metal railing (hotter than your hand) feels HOT, not cold — explain why the same good conductor now feels hot, separating the object's temperature from the DIRECTION energy flows.
State and defend a prediction, then revise the explanation in terms of what moves after seeing or reasoning through the outcome.
Trace how conduction, convection and radiation each play a part in a radiator heating a room.
Explain why a duvet keeps you warm even though it produces no heat of its own.
activities.insight: Articulating and defending predictions out loud surfaces the stubborn errors (cold flows in, metal is colder, radiation needs a medium, insulators give out heat) so they can be reframed around what actually moves and in which direction energy flows.

activities.title: Spatial convection loop and radiant spread
steps: Explore a room-scale convection loop you can orbit, following warmed, less-dense fluid rising and cooler fluid sinking.
Watch radiant infrared spreading outward from a source through space.
Compare this spatial view with the 2D cross-section and describe what each makes clearer.
activities.insight: Convection has a genuinely spatial circulating loop and radiation spreads outward in space; seeing this at room scale can make the circulation and spread feel natural.

checkQuestion: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have sat in the same room all day. The metal one feels colder to your hand. Are they actually at different temperatures? Explain why the metal feels colder even though both have been in the same room.
checkAnswer: No — both are at the same room temperature. The metal feels colder because it's a good conductor: it conducts heat away from your warm hand quickly, so your hand cools fast and feels the loss. Wood is a poor conductor, so it draws heat from your hand slowly and feels warmer. Feeling is about the RATE heat leaves your hand, not the object's temperature.
